title: Cheaper bread, less bread?
hook: Cap the price of bread so more people can afford it. What could go wrong?

knows: that people buy more of something when it is cheaper
reading a point on a graph

misconception: Lowering the price by rule means more people get the good, because more buyers can afford it.
objective: The learner can explain that the amount that changes hands is limited by both buyers and sellers, so at a capped price below the crossing point fewer units are sold and a shortage appears; in the model, the crossing price is where the most units change hands.

claims.text: The bread market in the lesson is an illustrative model with straight lines: buyers want 100 − 10 × price loaves a day and bakers bake 10 × price − 20, for prices from $2 to $10.
claims.source: The lesson's own made-up numbers (Demo.tsx). Linear demand and supply are the standard textbook simplification, e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 4.

claims.text: In the model the lines cross at $6, where buyers want and bakers bake 40 loaves a day.
No more can be sold than buyers want or bakers bake, so the number sold is the smaller of the two.
claims.source: The short-side rule of market models; Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 6 (with a binding price ceiling, quantity sold equals quantity supplied).

claims.text: With the price capped at $4, buyers want 60 loaves but bakers bake 20, so 20 are sold (down from 40) and 40 loaves are short.
In this model the number of loaves sold is largest at the crossing price.
claims.source: Sold = min(100 − 10p, 10p − 20): the first falls with p and the second rises, so the minimum peaks where they are equal (p = 6).

claims.text: In the standard model, a shortage pushes the price up and a surplus pushes it down, toward the crossing point.
claims.source: Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 4 (markets moving toward equilibrium).

claims.text: Real price caps can also bring effects this model leaves out, such as queues, black markets and lower quality.
claims.source: Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 6 (price ceilings, the rent control case study: shortages, waiting lines, black markets, reduced quality).

recall.question: A city caps the price of taxi rides well below today's price. In a simple supply and demand model, what happens to the number of rides taken?
options: It falls: fewer drivers offer rides
recall.why: A ride needs both a rider and a driver. At the lower price more people want rides but fewer drivers offer them, and only the rides offered can be taken.
